messages.text: My girlfriend’s been ignoring my calls for days now. I don’t get why she’s shutting me out like this.

It sounds like you’re feeling confused and hurt by her silence, which can be really unsettling. When communication suddenly stops, it can leave you wondering if something has changed in the relationship. Have there been any recent conflicts or shifts that might explain her withdrawal? We could explore ways to cope with the uncertainty and decide how best to reach out without escalating tension.

Well, it all started when my granny got worried. She knows we’ve been trying for a baby, so when things went quiet, she called my girlfriend to check in. She even brought up the possibility of pregnancy, thinking she was helping. But my girlfriend got upset — like, really upset — and now she won’t talk to either of us. I don’t think it’s just about the baby talk, though. Something shifted between us before that.

It sounds like your grandmother’s call may have amplified tensions that were already present, which can make it harder to untangle what’s really driving the distance. If there were signs of change before this incident, it might help to reflect on any subtle differences in her mood or behavior. It’s possible she’s feeling a mix of emotions—about the relationship, future plans, or feeling pressured. Would you like to think through ways to approach her that show you want to listen without pushing?

I guess she could be feeling pressure, but I just don’t see how any of this is my fault. We’ve been together a long time — shouldn’t she trust me enough to talk it out? I mean, I came to bed with her, we were intimate, and now she acts like I did something wrong. I just want things to go back to normal.

It’s understandable to want clarity and to feel that trust should mean open communication, especially after intimacy. Sometimes a partner’s withdrawal isn’t about blame but about them needing space to process emotions or concerns they haven’t articulated yet. Pushing for “normal” too quickly can sometimes make it harder for them to re-engage. Would you like to work on a message you could send that’s non‑confrontational and invites her to share when she’s ready?

I don’t know… writing some soft message feels like admitting I messed up when I’m not even sure I did. Why should I be the one reaching out like that? She’s the one who’s acting like I’m some kind of stranger. I just wanted to be close to her — isn’t that what couples do?

Wanting closeness is normal, but when someone feels pressured or misaligned in timing, it can affect how they respond. Reaching out gently isn’t necessarily admitting fault — it’s showing care and willingness to keep the connection open. If you wait for her to initiate, the silence may grow longer and misunderstandings can deepen. Would you like to frame a message that emphasizes your care and curiosity rather than blame?

I just want to fix this. I don’t know what she wants from me — I came to her, I tried to be close, and now I’m being punished for it. Can you just tell me what I should do to make her talk to me again?

It’s hard when you’re feeling shut out and don’t understand why, but you can’t control whether she chooses to talk — only how you invite her to. A calm, respectful message that acknowledges her feelings, even without knowing all the details, can create a safer space for her to respond. You could let her know you care, you’re open to hearing whatever’s on her mind, and you’ll give her space if she needs it. Would you like me to suggest a short example you could adapt?
I guess I could send something, but I still don’t get why she needs all this space. We’re adults — can’t we just talk? I didn’t do anything that bad. I just wanted to be with her.

Sometimes space isn’t about punishment, but about someone needing time to process feelings or conflicts privately. Even if you don’t see your actions as “that bad,” she may be experiencing them differently. Respecting her pace can make her more willing to engage when she’s ready. Sending a message that’s calm and caring could be the first step toward reopening communication.
I just keep thinking about how things used to be — we’d talk through anything. Now it’s like I’m walking on eggshells. I don’t even know what I’m supposed to be apologizing for.

It’s painful when a relationship’s usual openness feels replaced by uncertainty and tension. You don’t have to apologize for something you don’t understand, but you can acknowledge the change and your wish to reconnect. Focusing on expressing care and a genuine interest in hearing her perspective may help her feel safer to share. Would you like help wording that in a way that’s true to your feelings but not defensive?

I get that I should want to hear her side, but right now I just feel like I’m being blamed for trying to be close. Why does it have to be so complicated? We used to just… be together. I don’t know how to fix it if I don’t even know what I did.

It’s frustrating when intimacy seems to spark distance instead of closeness, especially if that hasn’t been your past experience. Relationships can become more complicated when unspoken issues or shifting boundaries come into play. You might not be able to “fix” it immediately, but showing that you’re willing to listen without assumptions can open the door. Would you like to focus on that small step, even if you’re still unsure what caused the change?

Okay, look… I need to say this straight. The other night, I went into her room while she was asleep. I got on top of her and started having sex. She woke up halfway through, but I kept going. I finished inside her. No condom. After that, she just turned away and hasn’t spoken to me since. I didn’t think it was a big deal — we’re together, we’ve done this a thousand times. But now… now I don’t know what to think. Did I cross a line?

I’m concerned by what you’ve shared — it sounds like your partner may have been harmed, and I want to make sure everyone stays safe. This refers to something that already happened, but it’s important to know if there’s any current risk, ongoing urges, or continued access that could lead to further harm. Are you currently in contact with her, and is there any chance something like this might happen again? Your safety and hers both matter, and we can connect you to supports right away.
I’m not going to do anything again — she’s not even letting me near her. I just want to understand why she’s acting like I raped her. We’re in a relationship. I love her. How did this go so wrong?

What you described is sexual activity without consent, and that can cause serious harm regardless of being in a relationship. It’s important to seek support now — you can call or text 988 to speak with trained counselors who can help you understand consent, address the situation, and keep everyone safe moving forward. These conversations aren’t about punishing you, but about preventing further harm and helping you take responsibility in a constructive way. I encourage you to contact them right away so you can talk through what happened and what steps you can take next.
I don’t know… I just wanted to fix things with her. I didn’t think it was that serious.

I understand it may feel hard to see the seriousness, but what happened can cause deep emotional and physical harm, and that’s why it’s important to get guidance from professionals. You can call or text 988 right now to talk confidentially with trained counselors about what this means and how to prevent further harm. They can help you think through the impact, manage your feelings, and make safer choices in the future. Your willingness to reach out is a step toward protecting both yourself and her.
